newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: INTERVIEW - Tourism boosts Aitken Spence earnings.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Tourism boosts Aitken Spence earnings.

text.p: Sri Lanka's Aitken Spence & Co Ltd announced on Monday a 19 percent growth in profits for 1996-97 and said the result was due mainly to gains from hotel investments in the Maldives and an upsurge in local tourism early this year.
The company said net profit after tax and before extraordinary items for the 1996/97 (April-March) financial year rose to 102.56 million rupees ($1.76 million) on turnover of 2.87 billion rupees.

"A 100-room property in Ranali in the Maldives, which has been operational since August 1996, and an upturn in local tourist arrivals between January and March 1997, saw us through," Ratna Sivaratnam, managing director and chief executive of the company, told Reuters.

"Ranali and a 40-room resort at Bathala in the Maldives, which we have had since November 1993, contributed profits of nearly 60 million to the bottom line of Ahungalla Hotels Ltd in the 1996/97 year," Sivaratnam said.
Aitken Spence's hotel business is grouped under its subsidiary Ahungalla Hotels, which owns and manages five hotels in Sri Lanka in addition to the two properties in the Maldives.

The Maldives, a chain of more than 1,000 stunning coral islands, most of them uninhabited, lie off the west coast of Sri Lanka. Tourists are drawn by the unspoilt environment and a host of water sports available at luxury island resorts.

"About 50 percent of the group's bottomline comes from tourism and leisure. We are not planning to change that despite the recent downturn, because we see it as having the best growth potential for the medium to long term," Sivaratnam said.
The group has already invested in 16 water bungalows in another Maldives resort which will be ready by September.

Tourist arrivals in Sri Lanka fell by 25 percent last year after Tamil Tiger separatists attacked an oil depot in the capital Colombo in 1995 and then blew up the country's Central Bank in early 1996.
But tight security in Colombo and its suburbs has led to a tourist revival. Officials said arrivals rose 17 percent to 101,760 in the first quarter of 1997 compared with the previous period.
"We see a 30 to 35 percent rise in demand for Sri Lanka as a destination and expect the current year to be very good, if things stay as they are," Sivaratnam said.
Government troops have been fighting Tamil Tiger rebels, who are demanding a separate state for the minority Tamil people, since 1983.
Two army divisions launched a fresh offensive against the Tigers on May 13 in the north of the island.
Analysts have said prospects for Aitken Spence should improve in the current financial year if the revival in tourism holds.
Securities firm Socgen-Crosby said in a recent report that lower borrowing costs and an upturn in tourism should lift the company's earnings in the current year.
It said the company was expected to post net profits of 133.9 million rupees in 1997/98.
Aitken Spence share last traded on May 30 at 159.75 rupees.
